Item 7 of Apple's fiscal 2024 Form 10-K (MD&A) names four results that weak foreign currencies against the U.S. dollar hurt, compared with fiscal 2023:

1. **Greater China net sales (renminbi).** The weak renminbi had an unfavorable year-over-year impact. Net sales fell 8%, from $72,559 million to $66,952 million. The filing attributes the decline mainly to lower iPhone and iPad sales.
2. **Japan net sales (yen).** The weak yen had an unfavorable year-over-year impact. Net sales still rose 3%, from $24,257 million to $25,052 million, mainly on higher iPhone sales.
3. **Rest of Asia Pacific net sales (foreign currencies generally).** The weakness in foreign currencies against the dollar had a "net unfavorable" year-over-year impact. No single currency is named. Net sales still rose 4%, from $29,615 million to $30,658 million, mainly on higher Services sales.
4. **Products gross margin and Products gross margin percentage (foreign currencies generally).** Both rose, from $108,803 million to $109,633 million and from 36.5% to 37.2%. Cost savings drove the increase. A different Products mix and the weakness in foreign currencies against the dollar partly offset it.

The MD&A does not attribute currency effects to Americas or Europe net sales, to the individual product categories, or to Services gross margin. It also does not quantify any of the currency effects in dollars.

The filing gives five percentages that fit your criteria.

| Percentage | What it measures |
|---|---|
| 40% | Share of fiscal 2025 total net sales made through direct distribution channels: Apple's retail and online stores and its direct sales force. |
| 60% | Share of fiscal 2025 total net sales made through indirect distribution channels, such as third-party cellular network carriers and other resellers. |
| 12% | Share of total trade receivables at September 27, 2025 owed by the one customer that represented 10% or more of those receivables. |
| 34% | Share of total trade receivables at September 27, 2025 owed by Apple's third-party cellular network carriers as a group. |
| 46% and 23% | Shares of total vendor non-trade receivables at September 27, 2025 held by each of the two vendors that individually represented 10% or more. |

- **Vendor non-trade receivables:** These arise when Apple sells components to manufacturing vendors that build subassemblies or assemble final products for it. Apple does not record these sales in products net sales. It recognizes any gain as a reduction of products cost of sales when the related final products are sold.
- **Unnamed counterparties:** The filing does not name the 12% customer or the two vendors. It also does not say whether the 12% customer is one of the carriers in the 34% group.
- **Different bases:** The percentages are measured against different totals (net sales, trade receivables and vendor non-trade receivables), so they can't be added together.

I left out the 10% reporting threshold. I also left out the prior-year comparatives: 38% for carriers, and 44% and 23% for the two vendors.

The filing dates five developments to 2025: four to a specific day and one to a month. They appear in Item 3 (Legal Proceedings) and in the Item 1A risk factor on regulatory scrutiny.

**April 23, 2025: EU Digital Markets Act (two developments)**
- **Article 5(4) investigation** (how developers communicate and promote offers to users and conclude contracts with them): The European Commission fined Apple €500 million. It also issued a cease-and-desist order requiring Apple to remove technical and commercial restrictions that stop developers from steering users to distribution channels outside the App Store. Apple has appealed.
- **Article 6(4) investigation** (whether Apple's new contractual requirements for third-party app developers and app marketplaces may violate the DMA): The Commission issued preliminary findings. A final violation finding could bring a cease-and-desist order and fines of up to 10% of Apple's annual worldwide net sales.

**April 30, 2025: Epic Games litigation (N.D. Cal.)**
- The court found Apple in violation of the 2021 Injunction.
- It barred Apple from imposing any commission or fee on purchases consumers make outside an app. It also barred Apple from restricting, conditioning, limiting or prohibiting how developers guide consumers to such purchases, and from otherwise interfering with a consumer's choice to proceed in or out of an app.
- It denied Apple's motion to narrow or vacate the injunction.
- It referred Apple to the U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of California to decide whether criminal contempt proceedings are appropriate.
- Apple appealed to the Ninth Circuit, and its request to stay the decision pending appeal was denied.

**September 2, 2025: Google search antitrust case (a commercial partner)**
- The U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia ordered certain remedies. This followed its August 5, 2024 finding that Google violated U.S. antitrust laws.
- The order is subject to further proceedings in that court and to appeal by both the DOJ and Google.
- The filing does not say what the remedies are.
- It warns that a reversal on appeal could bring remedies the DOJ originally proposed, such as barring Google from offering Apple commercial terms for search distribution. That could materially harm Apple's licensing revenue from these arrangements.

**October 2025: Epic Games appeal**
- The Ninth Circuit, which agreed to hear Apple's appeal on an expedited basis, heard oral arguments.

**Not counted because they are dated only by quarter or fall before 2025**
- Apple settled certain other matters in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2025. The filing gives only the quarter and says the settlements were not material.
- Apple's appeals of the EU decision and the April 30 ruling, and the stay denial, are described without dates.
- The DOJ smartphone monopolization suit (March 21, 2024), the opening of the two EU investigations (March 25 and June 24, 2024), the European Court of Justice State Aid ruling (September 10, 2024) and Google's liability finding (August 5, 2024) all predate 2025.

The filing covers this in the risk factors (p. 28) and the MD&A (p. 37). It describes these effects as having occurred or possibly having occurred:

1. **Products, services and support were blocked.** In response to the war, the U.S. and other jurisdictions imposed economic sanctions and export control measures. These "blocked the passage of our products, services and support into Russia, Belarus, and certain regions of Ukraine" (p. 28).
2. **Direct sales to Russia stopped.** NVIDIA stopped direct sales to Russia in fiscal 2023 (pp. 28, 37). The filing adds that direct sales to Russia in fiscal 2022 were immaterial (p. 37).
3. **Russian operations closed.** NVIDIA closed its business operations in Russia. The MD&A says this happened later in fiscal 2023 (pp. 28, 37).
4. **End customer sales in EMEA were affected.** The filing says the war "has impacted end customer sales in EMEA" (p. 28).
5. **Partner revenue may have been hurt.** Revenue from partners that sell into Russia "may have been negatively impacted due to the war in Ukraine" (p. 37). The filing treats this as possible, not confirmed.

- **Causation:** Items 2 and 3 appear in the same passage as the sanctions example. The filing does not separately state why NVIDIA took those steps.
- **No quantification:** The filing does not quantify any of these effects.
- **Excluded as future-only:** The statement that the war's impact on EMEA sales "may continue to do so in the future." Also the general statement that increasing use of economic sanctions "may also impact demand for our products or services."
- **Excluded as not tied to Ukraine:** The third-quarter fiscal 2023 U.S. license requirements on A100/H100 exports to China and Russia. The filing describes these as targeting China's semiconductor and supercomputing industries, not as a response to the war.

**Accounting change.** After the October 2024 sale, Pfizer lost significant influence over Haleon. It stopped using the equity method and now carries the stake at fair value. The filing also says Pfizer intends to sell its remaining Haleon investment during 2025.

All of these amounts come from JPMorgan Chase's January 1, 2023 adoption of the FASB's troubled debt restructuring (TDR) guidance, which it adopted under the modified retrospective method. Page numbers are the 10-K's printed pages.

**Allowance effects**

- **$587 million decrease, Firm-wide.** This is the net decrease in both the allowance for loan losses and the allowance for credit losses. It is a one-time cumulative-effect adjustment to the January 1, 2023 opening allowance, shown separately from the 2023 provision.
  - It results from dropping the TDR discounted-cash-flow measurement. Most modified loans to troubled borrowers moved to a portfolio-based approach. Collateral-dependent and nonaccrual risk-rated loans keep asset-specific measurement.
  - The 10-K says it was predominantly driven by residential real estate and credit card. I found no separate dollar figure for residential real estate.
  - The table shows no cumulative effect on the allowance for lending-related commitments, so the credit-loss and loan-loss effects are the same.
  - Sources: Note 1 (p. 173), Note 13 (pp. 256, 258), MD&A (pp. 58, 131–132).
- **The $587 million by loan portfolio** (Note 13, p. 258; MD&A, p. 132):
  - Consumer, excluding credit card: $489 million decrease.
  - Credit card: $100 million decrease.
  - Wholesale: $2 million increase.
- **$591 million decrease, Consumer & Community Banking (CCB) segment.** This is the net decrease in CCB's allowance for loan losses from the same adoption. It was "driven by residential real estate and credit card" (footnote to CCB selected metrics, p. 70).
  - It does not match the combined consumer decrease of $589 million ($489 million plus $100 million). The filing doesn't reconcile the two, and they group loans differently (a business segment versus loan-portfolio segments).

**Retained earnings effects**

- **$446 million increase, after tax.** This is the effect of adopting the TDR guidance on retained earnings at January 1, 2023. It is the counterpart of the allowance reduction, and it was predominantly driven by residential real estate and credit card. It is stated after tax, which is presumably why it is smaller than the $587 million allowance reduction. The filing doesn't give the tax amount (Note 1, p. 173; Note 13, p. 256).
- **$449 million increase.** This is the "Cumulative effect of change in accounting principles" line in the 2023 retained earnings rollforward (statement of changes in stockholders' equity, p. 169).
